Soon after we moved to this place where we live I noticed this small trace of yellow material in the kitchen granite counter. I definitely don't believe I just got rich, but considering it is an igneous rock, I believe there are remote chances of finding traces of precious materials in it.

Here are two pictures I took of it: http://slimgur.com/image/mcA http://slimgur.com/image/mcG

So my questions are: what material could it be? And what are the chances of this being gold?

Thanks!
Yellow material in my granite countertop. What could it be?

Chances of it being gold are slim to none - if the area where the granite is from has gold, that will be it primary export.

It's more than likely pyrite (fools gold) or chalcopyrite (fools gold but with some copper). After zooming in there are some obvious cube/square shaped crystals, strongly suggesting pyrite.
Either way, I think it is so cool! Thanks for the info! :)

No worries. There are lots of different types of granite (that have more specific names) and granite in the consumer world can mean a lot of different types. Depending on the crystal habit, colour, trace minerals, etc.

There is a good chance there's something radioactive in the counter-top too! (But not even as much as a banana so don't worry).
Definitely looks like pyrite. It's not uncommon in granites, but is usually oxidized to a rusty stain in pieces you might find on the ground.

Honestly, I'm loving the show. But deep down in my gut, I just get this nagging feeling that this show is going to end up sitting in my ultimate garbage pile.

1) It is a paint-by-numbers romance anime. While the pacing is definitely better than a lot of shows and it has flipped around the roles of main-cast bishie and side-cast comic relief, it definitely follows the ever popular formula for highschool romance series.

2) The manga is still ongoing. For those unaware with how the industry works, animes are made to promote the source material (the manga, in this case). Given that the ending for the manga hasn't been written yet, I have deep reservations for how good of an ending the anime will get. I am predicting a generic ending, or even a non-ending.

3) Romantic development is highly idealized for a romance show. There are "cute" misunderstandings, but very few if any fights or arguments.

4) The Mary Sue Effect. Takeo is so kind, so understanding, and so perfect that he is willing to accept a lot of possibilities. Seriously though, this extreme levels of kindness and compassion are nice, but it is bordering on either an extreme weakness of his, or an extreme superpower -- and so far the writing suggests that it's definitely not his Kryptonite.

Again, love the show. Sorry for the inane rambling, but the more episodes I watch of this show the more I resign myself to this show just being a guilty pleasure of oversaccharine romance.

A little bit, but not to the same extent.

The underlying problem is that as you age, your fluid memory decreases. What this essentially means is that it's harder to learn new things. Seniors who grew up without computers have nothing even remotely similar in their past to draw upon. The closest thing is probably TV, but that's not interactive at all.

Millennials on the other hand grew up with the stuff. So no matter what advancements happen to computers, they'll have a whole life of previous experience to draw upon. Think about how quickly you were able to use a smart phone for the first time, having your previous computer and cell phone experience to draw upon. Yes, it was groundbreaking, but you had a precedent for point a click functions, opening applications, etc.

I would imagine that if there are any technological advancements that are so immensely different and new from anything we currently have, then yes, Millennials will have just as many issues understanding it as current seniors do with computers.

Many are already. People understand consumer electronics UI, but not how things work.

The majority of the startup kids I know aren't even a little bit hacker, they're mostly iPhone.

The greater divide between those who grew up with the internet and those who didn't is already occurring, socially. Children who grew up with the internet available at a young age think differently. They were the first generation who could spontaneously provide answers to any question, the first generation to throw privacy out the window via social media, and they have become used to instant gratification, rushing into all kinds of relationship with an openness that is representative of what it means to be a "millennial."

Though I am a millennial myself, I consider myself lucky to have grown up before smart phones, vine, buzzfeed, and the like. It seems to me that this generational gap will continue to widen as new forms of 6-second, thoughtless entertainment emerge, shifting entertainment from an emphasis on developing a compelling plot, an immersive world, and believable characters, to a purely aesthetic model, relying on flashing lights, explosions, and tits.

Many millenials are already technologically oblivious, they use it while having no idea what they're doing.

It depends on what new technology concepts are introduced. Outside of the GUI, there hasn't been that much change in technology in terms of how people interact with it.
I'm seeing a whole generation that can operate Facebook and snapchat, but can't change a car tire. Can't change their oil. Can't fix anything mechanical.
I could change a car tire and do those other things... After watching three youtube videos and reading two how-to guides where they explain it extensively.
My 19 year old daughter said the lawnmower was broken and demanded I buy another one. Out of gas.

I think we've become so accustomed to things around us changing so rapidly, that we're never going to be caught off-guard, even if there is another huge paradigm shift. We're highly adaptable, and while only a few know the technical ins-and-outs of how technologies actually function, I think we will progress towards greater complexity seamlessly.

Plus, the intense overstimulation of our minds with novelty at all times while we're young is a factor in the argument that neuro-degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's will be less prevelant in millenials.

Something else will sneak up on us, we'll never see it coming and the only ones who understand it will be the ones using whatever it is in their careers. I've always feared genetic engineering making the next generation all 200+iq catalog models. Thus, making me close to a neanderthal by comparison.

If the current market trends of making technological products sealed and self-contained continues, definitely. Nobody has the ability to maintain a collection of a bunch of independent, unrelated, un-investigable products in working order in their heads.

While I firmly believe that nobody should have to put together their own computer (hardware or software) from scratch any more than they should have to assemble their own car, doing so should always be an option and you should be able to open the goddamn hood and mess with it as needed. I've seen cars where the whole engine bay is under wraps and only the battery terminals and oil inlet are exposed. Anything else breaks, go to the dealer. If that was someone's first car, they'd be mechanically oblivious. Our computers are like that (looking at you, Apple) and so we're accustomed to them using us as much as us using them, and god help us if exceptions arise.

As far as our ability to learn and use tools goes, though, nah man that's what humans are awesome at. The technologically oblivious seniors among us tend to be those who aren't great at pushing their comfort zones and didn't have exposure to this sort of thing growing up, so they're both uncertain and unwilling to explore. My mom is 60 and still uses MS Office 2003 and a landline; my dad is 63 and only needs me to do really obscure (relative to us) tweaks when something goes wrong. Mom majored in German and was a flight attendant until I was born, then went full-time mother. Dad was a mathematician, Navy fighter pilot, civilian fighter pilot, and now an FAA worker. She's never had to interact with technology beyond getting the basics of what she needed done; dad's been surrounded by it and depended on it to keep him alive for years.

I figure as long as technology has such a prevalent role in our lives, we'll continue to be okay with it. To extend my car metaphor from above, we still have 80-year-olds on the roads, because even they grew up with cars. They might not be awesome at it, but as long as they're physically healthy they can generally still manage it safely. That'll be us with computers.
